questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the type of clause underlined in the sentence: 'I know WHAT HE SAID at the meeting.'
questions.explanation: 'What he said at the meeting' functions as the object of the verb 'know', making it a noun clause. An adjective clause is wrong — it would modify a noun; an adverb clause is wrong — it would modify a verb with time/reason/condition; a main clause is wrong — it cannot stand alone as the complete sentence.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about noun clauses:

(i) A noun clause can function as the subject of a sentence.
(ii) A noun clause can function as the object of a verb.
(iii) A noun clause always begins with 'because' or 'although'.
(iv) A noun clause can follow a preposition.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Noun clauses can be subjects (i-correct, e.g., 'What he said surprised me'), objects (ii-correct, e.g., 'I know what he wants'), and follow prepositions (iv-correct, e.g., 'I am interested in what she proposes'). Statement (iii) is wrong because 'because' and 'although' introduce adverb clauses, not noun clauses. Noun clauses typically begin with 'that', 'what', 'who', 'whether', etc.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence that contains an adjective clause:
options: She asked whether I could help her.
The book that I borrowed is very interesting.
After the rain stopped, we went outside.
I believe that honesty is important.
questions.correctAnswer: The book that I borrowed is very interesting.
questions.explanation: 'That I borrowed' modifies the noun 'book', making it an adjective clause. 'Whether I could help her' is wrong — it's a noun clause (object of 'asked'); 'After the rain stopped' is wrong — it's an adverb clause of time; 'that honesty is important' is wrong — it's a noun clause (object of 'believe').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The clause 'because he was tired' is an adverb clause.
Reason (R): It modifies the verb in the main clause by providing the reason for the action.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Because he was tired' is indeed an adverb clause (A is correct). It modifies the verb by explaining the reason/cause for the action (R is correct and directly explains why it's classified as an adverb clause). Option 2 is wrong because R precisely explains A; Option 3 is wrong because R is factually correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is also correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences contains a noun clause functioning as the subject?

(i) What she told me was shocking.
(ii) That he passed the exam made everyone happy.
(iii) I don't know where he lives.
(iv) The man who called is my uncle.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'What she told me' is the subject of 'was shocking' (i-correct); 'That he passed the exam' is the subject of 'made' (ii-correct). 'Where he lives' (iii) is wrong — it functions as an object, not a subject; 'who called' (iv) is wrong — it's an adjective clause modifying 'man', not a noun clause.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the adjective clause in the sentence: 'The teacher who taught us English has retired.'
questions.explanation: 'Who taught us English' is an adjective clause modifying the noun 'teacher'. 'The teacher' is wrong — it is just a noun phrase; 'has retired' is wrong — it is the predicate of the main clause; 'us English' is wrong — it is just a part of the adjective clause itself.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following clauses with their types:

Column I:
(a) wherever you go
(b) that he is innocent
(c) which was built in 1920
(d) before the sun sets

Column II:
(i) Adjective clause
(ii) Adverb clause of place
(iii) Noun clause
(iv) Adverb clause of time

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Wherever you go' indicates place (a-ii); 'that he is innocent' is a noun clause (b-iii, typically object of a verb like 'believe'); 'which was built in 1920' modifies a noun (c-i); 'before the sun sets' indicates time (d-iv). Option 2 swaps place and time; Option 3 swaps noun and adjective; Option 4 assigns noun to 'wherever'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The clause 'although she studied hard' is an example of:
questions.explanation: 'Although she studied hard' is an adverb clause of concession (showing contrast/unexpected result). A noun clause is wrong — it doesn't function as subject/object; an adjective clause is wrong — it doesn't modify a noun; an adverb clause of condition is wrong — 'although' shows concession, not condition (conditions use 'if/unless').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about adjective clauses:

(i) An adjective clause modifies a noun or pronoun.
(ii) Adjective clauses are introduced by relative pronouns like who, which, that, whom, whose.
(iii) An adjective clause always comes before the noun it modifies.
(iv) A restrictive adjective clause provides essential information to identify the noun.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Adjective clauses modify nouns/pronouns (i-correct), are introduced by relative pronouns (ii-correct), and restrictive ones give essential identification (iv-correct). Statement (iii) is wrong because adjective clauses come AFTER the noun they modify, not before (e.g., 'The man WHO LIVES NEXT DOOR is friendly').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence that contains an adverb clause of condition:
options: I will help you if you ask me politely.
She cried because she lost her keys.
He ran so fast that he won the race.
When the bell rings, the students leave.
questions.correctAnswer: I will help you if you ask me politely.
questions.explanation: 'If you ask me politely' is an adverb clause of condition (states a condition for the main action). 'Because she lost her keys' is wrong — it's an adverb clause of reason; 'so fast that he won' is wrong — it's an adverb clause of result; 'When the bell rings' is wrong — it's an adverb clause of time.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'Where he keeps his money' can function as a noun clause.
Reason (R): A noun clause can begin with a 'wh-' word and perform the function of a noun in a sentence.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Where he keeps his money' can be a noun clause (e.g., 'Nobody knows where he keeps his money' — object of 'knows') (A is correct). Noun clauses can begin with wh-words and perform noun functions (R is correct and explains A). Option 2 is wrong because R directly explains how A works; Option 3 is wrong because R is factually correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'The house where I was born has been demolished', the clause 'where I was born' is:
questions.explanation: 'Where I was born' modifies the noun 'house' (tells us WHICH house), so it is an adjective clause. A noun clause is wrong — it doesn't function as subject/object; an adverb clause of place is wrong — it modifies a noun, not a verb; a main clause is wrong — it is subordinate.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct clause type: In 'She said that she would come tomorrow,' the underlined clause functions as a __________ clause.
questions.explanation: 'That she would come tomorrow' is the object of the verb 'said', functioning as a noun clause. Adjective is wrong — it doesn't modify a noun; adverb is wrong — it doesn't modify the verb with time/reason/condition; main is wrong — it is a subordinate (dependent) clause.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following are subordinating conjunctions that introduce adverb clauses?

(i) because
(ii) which
(iii) although
(iv) unless

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Because' (reason), 'although' (concession), and 'unless' (condition) all introduce adverb clauses (i, iii, iv correct). 'Which' (ii) is wrong because it is a relative pronoun that introduces adjective clauses or noun clauses, not adverb clauses.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the noun clause in the sentence: 'Whether he will come to the party is still uncertain.'
options: Whether he will come to the party
questions.correctAnswer: Whether he will come to the party
questions.explanation: 'Whether he will come to the party' is the subject of the sentence (noun clause functioning as subject). 'He will come' is wrong — it's only part of the clause; 'to the party' is wrong — it's a prepositional phrase; 'is still uncertain' is wrong — it's the predicate of the main clause.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentences with the type of adverb clause they contain:

Column I:
(a) He works hard so that he may succeed.
(b) If it rains, the match will be cancelled.
(c) She is taller than her sister is.
(d) Wherever you go, I will follow.

Column II:
(i) Adverb clause of condition
(ii) Adverb clause of purpose
(iii) Adverb clause of place
(iv) Adverb clause of comparison

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'So that he may succeed' shows purpose (a-ii); 'If it rains' shows condition (b-i); 'than her sister is' shows comparison (c-iv); 'Wherever you go' shows place (d-iii). Option 2 swaps purpose and condition; Option 3 swaps condition and comparison; Option 4 swaps comparison and place.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'I don't believe what he says', the clause 'what he says' functions as:
questions.explanation: 'What he says' is the direct object of 'believe' (noun clause as object). 'Subject' is wrong — 'I' is the subject; 'complement' is wrong — it doesn't describe the subject; 'adverb' is wrong — it doesn't modify how/when/why someone believes.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about adverb clauses:

(i) An adverb clause modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb.
(ii) Adverb clauses can express time, place, reason, condition, purpose, result, or concession.
(iii) Adverb clauses are introduced by subordinating conjunctions.
(iv) An adverb clause always comes after the main clause.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Adverb clauses modify verbs/adjectives/adverbs (i-correct), express various relationships (ii-correct), and are introduced by subordinating conjunctions (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because adverb clauses can come BEFORE the main clause (e.g., 'When I arrived, he had left') or after it.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence that contains a noun clause functioning as a complement:
options: The problem is that we have no money.
The girl who won the prize is my cousin.
He left because he was angry.
I will go wherever you send me.
questions.correctAnswer: The problem is that we have no money.
questions.explanation: 'That we have no money' follows the linking verb 'is' and describes the subject 'problem' — it's a noun clause as subject complement (predicate nominative). 'Who won the prize' is wrong — it's an adjective clause; 'because he was angry' is wrong — it's an adverb clause; 'wherever you send me' is wrong — it's an adverb clause of place.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the sentence 'The car which my father bought is red', the clause 'which my father bought' is an adjective clause.
Reason (R): It modifies the noun 'car' by providing additional identifying information about it.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Which my father bought' is indeed an adjective clause (A is correct). It modifies 'car' by identifying which car (R is correct and explains A). Option 2 is wrong because R gives the exact reason for the classification; Option 3 is wrong because R is factually correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is also correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The clause 'so that everyone could hear' in the sentence 'He spoke loudly so that everyone could hear' is:
questions.explanation: 'So that everyone could hear' expresses purpose — why he spoke loudly. A noun clause is wrong — it doesn't function as subject/object; an adjective clause is wrong — it doesn't modify a noun; an adverb clause of result is wrong — result clauses use 'so...that' pattern (e.g., 'so loudly that everyone heard'), while purpose uses 'so that + may/could'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences contain adjective clauses?

(i) The man whose car was stolen reported to the police.
(ii) I know where she lives.
(iii) The film that we watched yesterday was boring.
(iv) He told me that he was leaving.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Whose car was stolen' modifies 'man' (i-correct adjective clause); 'that we watched yesterday' modifies 'film' (iii-correct adjective clause). 'Where she lives' (ii) is wrong — it's a noun clause (object of 'know'); 'that he was leaving' (iv) is wrong — it's a noun clause (object of 'told').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'Whoever finishes first will get a prize', the noun clause is:
questions.explanation: 'Whoever finishes first' is the subject of the sentence (noun clause as subject). 'Will get a prize' is wrong — it's the predicate; 'first will get' is wrong — it's a meaningless fragment; 'a prize' is wrong — it's just a noun phrase.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following subordinating conjunctions with the type of adverb clause they introduce:

Column I:
(a) because
(b) until
(c) as if
(d) provided that

Column II:
(i) Adverb clause of condition
(ii) Adverb clause of manner
(iii) Adverb clause of time
(iv) Adverb clause of reason

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces reason (a-iv); 'until' introduces time (b-iii); 'as if' introduces manner (c-ii); 'provided that' introduces condition (d-i). Option 2 swaps time and reason; Option 3 swaps time and manner; Option 4 swaps manner and condition.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the sentence 'It is important that you arrive on time':

(i) 'That you arrive on time' is a noun clause.
(ii) It functions as the subject of the sentence (delayed subject).
(iii) 'It' is an expletive (dummy subject) in this sentence.
(iv) 'That you arrive on time' is an adjective clause modifying 'important'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'That you arrive on time' is a noun clause (i-correct), it functions as the real/delayed subject (ii-correct), and 'It' is an expletive/dummy subject standing in for the clause (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because it is a noun clause, not an adjective clause — it doesn't modify 'important'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The word 'that' introduces a noun clause in which of the following sentences?
options: The book that you lent me is excellent.
I hope that you will succeed.
The fact that he knew surprised everyone.
questions.explanation: In 'I hope that you will succeed', 'that you will succeed' is a noun clause (object of 'hope'). In 'The fact that he knew surprised everyone', 'that he knew' is a noun clause in apposition to 'fact'. In 'The book that you lent me', 'that' introduces an adjective clause modifying 'book'. So both B and C have noun clauses.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A non-restrictive adjective clause is set off by commas.
Reason (R): Non-restrictive clauses provide additional but non-essential information that can be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Non-restrictive clauses are set off by commas (A is correct). Because they add extra, removable information (not essential for identification), commas signal this to the reader (R is correct and explains A). Option 2 is wrong because R explains exactly why commas are used; Option 3 is wrong because R is factually correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is also correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence that contains an adverb clause of time:
options: She dances as if she were a professional.
We waited until the train arrived.
He studies hard so that he may pass.
The reason why he failed is clear.
questions.correctAnswer: We waited until the train arrived.
questions.explanation: 'Until the train arrived' tells WHEN the waiting ended — an adverb clause of time. 'As if she were a professional' is wrong — it's manner; 'so that he may pass' is wrong — it's purpose; 'why he failed' is wrong — it's a noun clause (or adjective clause modifying 'reason').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the difference between adjective and adverb clauses:

(i) Adjective clauses modify nouns; adverb clauses modify verbs, adjectives, or adverbs.
(ii) Adjective clauses are introduced by relative pronouns; adverb clauses by subordinating conjunctions.
(iii) Both adjective and adverb clauses are types of subordinate clauses.
(iv) Adjective clauses always begin with 'because' or 'when'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Adjective clauses modify nouns while adverb clauses modify verbs/adjectives/adverbs (i-correct); adjective clauses use relative pronouns, adverb clauses use subordinating conjunctions (ii-correct); both are subordinate clauses (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because 'because' and 'when' introduce ADVERB clauses, not adjective clauses.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'I am not sure whether she will accept the offer', the noun clause functions as:
questions.explanation: 'Whether she will accept the offer' completes the meaning of the adjective 'sure' — it is a noun clause functioning as complement of the adjective. 'Subject' is wrong — 'I' is the subject; 'object of accept' is wrong — 'the offer' is the object of 'accept'; 'adverb' is wrong — it doesn't modify the manner/degree of 'sure'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the appropriate subordinating conjunction: __________ he is rich, he is not happy.
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces an adverb clause of concession — showing contrast between being rich and being unhappy. 'Because' is wrong — it would mean his richness causes unhappiness (illogical); 'Unless' is wrong — it introduces condition and doesn't fit the contrast; 'When' is wrong — it introduces time, not concession.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Which of the following relative pronouns is used to introduce adjective clauses referring to PEOPLE?
questions.explanation: Both 'who' and 'that' can introduce adjective clauses for people (e.g., 'The man who/that helped me'). 'Which' is wrong for people — it's used for things; 'Who' alone is partially correct but incomplete since 'that' also works; 'That' alone is also partially correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following noun clauses with their grammatical functions:

Column I:
(a) What he wants is unclear.
(b) I believe that he is honest.
(c) The truth is that she lied.
(d) Give it to whoever needs it.

Column II:
(i) Object of a verb
(ii) Subject of the sentence
(iii) Subject complement
(iv) Object of a preposition

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'What he wants' is the subject (a-ii); 'that he is honest' is object of 'believe' (b-i); 'that she lied' follows linking verb 'is' as complement (c-iii); 'whoever needs it' is object of preposition 'to' (d-iv). Option 2 swaps subject and object; Option 3 swaps object and complement; Option 4 swaps complement and preposition object.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The clause 'as though he had seen a ghost' in the sentence 'He trembled as though he had seen a ghost' is an adverb clause of:
questions.explanation: 'As though he had seen a ghost' describes HOW he trembled — an adverb clause of manner. Reason is wrong — that would use 'because'; condition is wrong — that would use 'if/unless'; time is wrong — that would use 'when/while'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the word 'where' in clauses:

(i) 'Where' can introduce an adverb clause of place (e.g., 'Go where you are sent').
(ii) 'Where' can introduce a noun clause (e.g., 'I don't know where he lives').
(iii) 'Where' can introduce an adjective clause (e.g., 'The city where I was born is small').
(iv) 'Where' always introduces an adverb clause.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Where' can introduce an adverb clause of place (i-correct), a noun clause as object (ii-correct), or an adjective clause modifying a noun of place (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because 'where' can introduce all three types of subordinate clauses depending on context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence in which 'that' introduces an adjective clause:
options: I know that she is coming.
The idea that he proposed was brilliant.
It is clear that we need more time.
She believes that hard work pays off.
questions.correctAnswer: The idea that he proposed was brilliant.
questions.explanation: In 'The idea that he proposed', 'that he proposed' modifies the noun 'idea' (adjective clause — WHICH idea?). In all other options, 'that' introduces noun clauses: 'that she is coming' (object of 'know'), 'that we need more time' (delayed subject), 'that hard work pays off' (object of 'believes').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences contains an adverb clause of result?

(i) He was so tired that he fell asleep immediately.
(ii) She worked hard so that she could pass.
(iii) The noise was so loud that we could not hear each other.
(iv) If you work hard, you will succeed.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'So tired that he fell asleep' (i) and 'so loud that we could not hear' (iii) show result (so...that pattern). 'So that she could pass' (ii) is wrong — it shows purpose (not result); 'If you work hard' (iv) is wrong — it shows condition.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: In the sentence 'Tell me who broke the window', the noun clause 'who broke the window' functions as:
questions.explanation: 'Who broke the window' is what you are being asked to tell — it's the direct object of 'tell'. 'Subject' is wrong — 'you (understood)' is the subject; 'indirect object' is wrong — 'me' is the indirect object; 'subject complement' is wrong — there's no linking verb.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the sentence 'The boy whom we met yesterday is my classmate':

(i) 'Whom we met yesterday' is an adjective clause.
(ii) It modifies the noun 'boy'.
(iii) 'Whom' is used because it functions as the object within the clause.
(iv) This clause is an adverb clause of time because it mentions 'yesterday'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Whom we met yesterday' is an adjective clause (i-correct), modifies 'boy' (ii-correct), and 'whom' is the object form of 'who' because it's the object of 'met' (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because the mere presence of 'yesterday' doesn't make it an adverb clause — it modifies a noun ('boy'), so it's an adjective clause.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Select the sentence that contains a noun clause in apposition:
options: I wonder who will win the match.
The belief that the earth is flat is wrong.
She studies when she has time.
The dog that bit him was caught.
questions.correctAnswer: The belief that the earth is flat is wrong.
questions.explanation: 'That the earth is flat' is a noun clause in apposition to 'belief' — it explains what the belief is. 'Who will win' is wrong — it's a noun clause as object; 'when she has time' is wrong — it's an adverb clause; 'that bit him' is wrong — it's an adjective clause modifying 'dog'.
